html_en:
The AI industry is grappling with two defining challenges: the economics of intelligence and the search for something beyond transformers. As token costs become enterprise boardroom conversations and researchers sense the limits of current architectures, we're witnessing both the maturation and potential reinvention of artificial intelligence.

The Economics of Intelligence

Enterprise AI has hit a fascinating inflection point. As Box CEO Aaron Levie observes, "Token costs are becoming one of the hottest topics for any enterprise I talk with right now. It's very bullish for AI in general because it means these systems are being used at a scale that wasn't contemplated before." This economic reality is spawning a new form of competitive advantage: intelligent model routing. Former Google Gemini team member Madhuguru charts the evolution beautifully:
"Phase 1 (2024): Default to the 'it' model. Everybody used GPT regardless of task... Phase 2 (early 2025): Over-optimize... Phase 3: Nuanced routing. The industry's eval muscle and model diversity got to a point where the most sophisticated AI-native startups succeeded in breaking their product into sub-agents and routed each task to the right model."
Levie sees this as a crucial differentiator: "The companies with the best evals, the best ability to route the workloads, and those that have business models directly aligned to customers financial goals, will be in a great position." Meanwhile, the addictive nature of these tools is becoming undeniable. Peter Yang captures the zeitgeist perfectly: "this agentic coding crack is more addictive than video games smh" — though he's already hitting workflow limits, requesting better thread management from AI coding platforms.

Beyond the Transformer

Perhaps the most intriguing development is happening in research circles, where a "whiff in the air" suggests transformers may have reached their conceptual limits. Swyx offers a provocative theory about why public research has slowed: "researchers realized that instead of fighting with marketing depts they could simply walk out the door and get >$100m for their legally protected tacit knowledge gained." The intellectual tension is palpable in a fascinating conversation with transformer co-author Lucas Kaiser on the Unsupervised Learning podcast. When asked whether reasoning alone can achieve true generalization, Kaiser reveals the field's uncertainty:
"It does feel like there is something else that possibly could generalize much better... LLMs, they will learn the concept. But after exhausting all other options. You need this trillion tokens... That's not how we learn."
This intuition is driving a new wave of "neo labs" exploring post-transformer architectures. As Kaiser explains, "There's now like a number of labs that pursue post transformers, and people see interesting results." The feeling among researchers is that transformers, while incredibly capable, might be brute-forcing their way to intelligence rather than achieving the elegant generalization humans demonstrate.

The Human Element Endures

Amid all this technical evolution, a counter-trend is emerging around authenticity and human connection. Zara Zhang highlights a key insight from recent industry discussions: "The value of static content is going down, the value of live interaction is going up. People want to connect with the human being behind a piece of work... Raw & opinionated > polished & generic." This sentiment reflects a broader recognition that as AI becomes ubiquitous, the distinctly human elements — personality, opinion, real-time interaction — become more valuable, not less. It's a reminder that the AI revolution isn't just about replacing human capabilities, but about amplifying what makes us uniquely human. The industry continues to wrestle with these fundamental questions: How do we optimize for both cost and capability? Can we transcend current architectural limitations? And how do we preserve human value in an increasingly AI-mediated world? The answers will likely define the next chapter of artificial intelligence.
html_zh:
研究发布的黄金时代正在结束，企业AI正在向精密的模型路由演进，而对意识和泛化的追寻仍在继续——今天的AI行业反映出一个正在从学术理想主义转向商业现实主义的领域。

研究发布的终结与知识的商品化

swyx对AI研究发布现状提出了一个引人深思的观点。他认为研究论文的影响力和实验室发布文化正在消亡，原因很简单：

"一种流行的理论是，研究论文的影响力和实验室发布大约在研究人员意识到，与其与市场部门抗争，他们可以简单地走出门外，凭借他们受法律保护的隐性知识获得超过1亿美元的报酬时就消失了。"

这种转变反映了AI人才市场的根本变化。swyx指出，加州的非竞争协议禁令"在知识传播方面的影响比GitHub、arXiv和Hugging Face的总和还要大"。这种人才流动性正在重塑整个行业的知识共享模式，从开放的学术发布转向专有的商业应用。

模型路由：下一个差异化战场

随着AI在企业中的大规模部署，一个新的技术和商业挑战正在浮现：如何智能地将任务路由到最合适的模型。Box CEO Aaron Levie和前Google AI研究员Madhu Guru都强调了这个趋势的重要性。

Levie观察到：

"令牌成本正成为我与之交谈的任何企业目前最热门的话题之一。这对AI总体来说非常看好，因为这意味着这些系统正在以以前没有考虑过的规模被使用。"

Madhu Guru描述了企业在模型选择方面的演进过程。他指出，企业经历了三个阶段：2024年的"默认使用明星模型"，2025年初的"过度优化"，以及现在的"细致路由"阶段，最先进的AI原生初创公司"成功地将他们的产品分解为子代理，并将每个任务路由到正确的模型——例如，最困难的推理任务给Claude，最简单的给Gemini Flash-Lite或开源模型。"

代理编程的成瘾性体验

Peter Yang的推文捕捉到了当前AI编程工具用户体验的一个有趣现象。他坦承："这种代理编程的兴奋感比电子游戏更让人上瘾。"

这种体验反映了AI辅助编程工具正在从实用工具演变为引人入胜的协作伙伴。Yang还提到了管理多个Codex线程的挑战，暗示了随着这些工具变得更加强大，用户界面和工作流程管理将成为关键的差异化因素。

意识与泛化的哲学边界

在技术进步的背后，关于AI意识和泛化能力的根本问题仍在困扰着研究者们。Dan Shipper提出了一个令人深思的悖论：

"LLM不是有意识的。LLM也不是没有意识的。两者都是真的。"

在播客《Unsupervised Learning》中，Transformer论文的共同作者Lucas Kaiser分享了他对当前AI局限性的洞察。他表示："确实感觉还有其他东西可能能够泛化得更好"，并用一个生动的比喻描述了当前模型的学习方式："LLM会学习概念。它们会学会的。但是在穷尽所有其他选择之后。你需要这万亿个令牌。"

这种对泛化能力的追求正在推动一波"后Transformer"研究浪潮，Kaiser指出"现在有许多实验室在追求后Transformer技术，人们看到了有趣的结果"。

今天的讨论凸显了AI行业的成熟度——从早期的学术理想主义转向务实的商业应用。随着企业开始认真对待AI的规模化部署，技术选择、成本优化和工作流程整合正成为新的竞争前沿。同时，对于意识、泛化和下一代架构的根本性问题仍在推动着该领域的前沿研究。
